column1: #Text=It is a remarkable fact that the toughest flesh-meat, if boiled with
#Text= the herb, or with other kindred docks, will become quite tender.
#Text=The name Patience, or Passions, was probably from the Italian
#Text= _Lapazio_, a corruption of _Lapathum_, which was mistaken for
#Text= _la passio_, the passion of Christ.
#Text=Our _Garden Rhubarb_ is a true Dock, and belongs to the "many-kneed,"
#Text= buckwheat order of plants.
#Text=Its brilliant colouring is due to
#Text= varying states of its natural pigment (chlorophyll), in
#Text= combination with oxygen.
#Text=For culinary purposes the stalk, or
#Text= petiole of the broad leaf, is used.
#Text=Its chief nutrient property is
#Text= glucose, which is identical with grape-sugar.
#Text=The agreeable taste
#Text= and odour of the  plant are not brought out until the leaf
#Text= stalks are cooked.
#Text=It came originally from the Volga, and has been
#Text= grown in this country since 1573.

#Text=Gum Sandarach, or Pounce, is the product of this tree.
#Text=Medicinally, the berries and the fragrant tops are employed.
#Text=They
#Text= contain "juniperin," sugar, resins, wax, fat, formic and acetic acids,
#Text= and malates.
#Text=The fresh tops have a balsamic odour, and a
#Text= carminative, bitterish taste.
#Text=The berries afford a yellow aromatic oil,
#Text= which acts on the kidneys, and gives cordial warmth to the stomach.
#Text=Forty berries should yield an ounce of the oil.
#Text=Steeped in alcohol the
#Text= berries make a capital _ratafia_; they are used in several
#Text= confections, as well as for flavouring gin, being put into a spirit
#Text= more common than the true geneva of Holland.
#Text=The French obtain
#Text= from these berries the _Genièvre_ (Anglice_ "geneva"), from
#Text= which we have taken our English word "gin."
#Text=In France, Savoy, and
#Text= Italy, the berries are largely collected, and are sometimes eaten as
#Text= such, fifteen or twenty at a time, to stimulate the kidneys; or they
#Text= are taken in powder for the same  purpose.
#Text=Being fragrant of
#Text= smell, they have a warm, sweet, pungent flavour, which becomes
#Text= bitter on further mastication.

#Text=Wormwood; but the odour of Mugwort is not fragrant or aromatic,
#Text= because it does not possess a volatile essential oil like that of the
#Text= _Artemisia absinthium_ (Wormwood).
#Text=This Wormwood is also a Composite plant of the same tribe and
#Text= character, but with an intensely bitter taste; and hence its name,
#Text= _Absinthium_, has been derived from the Greek privative, _a_, and
#Text= _psinthos_, "delight," because the flavour is so bitterly distasteful.
#Text=It is a bushy plant, which abounds in our rural districts, having silky
#Text= stems and leaves, with small heads of dull yellow flowers, the whole
#Text= plant being _amara et aromatica_.
#Text=The Mugwort, as an allied Wormwood of the same genus, is taller
#Text= and more slender than the Absinthium, and is distinguished by being
#Text= scentless, its leaves being green above, and white below.
#Text=The bitter
#Text= taste of the true Wormwood is also due to "absinthin," and each
#Text= kind contains nitrate of potash, tannin, and resin, with succinic,
#Text= malic, and acetic acids.
#Text=It quickly induces a sharp burning pain, and it excites a destructive

#Text=Officinally the tree is named _Myristica officinalis_, and the oil
#Text= distilled from the Nutmeg in Britain is much superior to foreign oil.
#Text=Ordinarily as a condiment of a warming character the Nutmeg is
#Text= employed to correct cold indigestible food, or as a cordial addition
#Text= to negus: and medicinally for languid digestion, with giddiness and
#Text= flatulence, causing oppressed breathing.
#Text=Its activity depends on the
#Text= volatile oil, contained in the proportion of six per cent. in the nut.
#Text=This when given at all largely is essentially narcotic.
#Text=Four Nutmegs
#Text= have been known to completely paralyse all nervous sensibility, and
#Text= have produced a sort of wakeful unconsciousness for three entire
#Text= days, with loss of memory afterwards, and with more or less
#Text= paralysis until after eight days.
#Text=The Banda, or Nutmeg Islands in the Indian Ocean, are twelve in
#Text= number, and the strength of the Nutmeg in its season is said to
#Text= overcome birds of Paradise so that they fall helplessly intoxicated.

#Text=The Orange flowers yield a
#Text= volatile, odorous oil, acetic acid, and acetate of lime.
#Text=The juice of
#Text= the Orange consists of citric and malic acids, with sugar;
#Text= citrate of lime, and water.
#Text=The peel furnishes hesperidin, a volatile
#Text= oil, gallic acid, and a bitter principle.
#Text=By druggists, a confection of bitter orange peel is sold; also a syrup
#Text= of this orange peel, and a tincture of the same, made with spirit of
#Text= wine, to be given in doses of from one to two teaspoonfuls with
#Text= water, as an agreeable stomachic bitter.
#Text=_Eau de Cologne_ contains
#Text= oil of neroli, oil of citron, and oil of orange.
#Text=The fresh juice of Oranges is antiseptic, and will prevent scurvy if
#Text= taken in moderation daily.
#Text=Common Oranges cut through the middle
#Text= while green, and dried in the air, being afterwards steeped for forty
#Text= days in oil, are used by the Arabs for preparing an essence famous
#Text= among their old women because it will restore a fresh dark, or
#Text= black colour to grey hair.

#Text=It contains an essential oil and a bitter resin, which
#Text= are useful as warmly carminative to relieve flatulent indigestion, and
#Text= to promote the monthly flow in women.
#Text=An infusion of the herb is
#Text= made, and given in two tablespoonfuls for a dose.
#Text=Cows which feed
#Text= on this plant have their flow of milk increased thereby.
#Text=Small
#Text= bunches of the leaves and shoots when tied together and suspended
#Text= in a cask of beer impart to it an agreeable aromatic flavour, and are
#Text= thought to correct tart, or spoiled wines.
#Text=The root, when fresh,
#Text= has a hot pungent bitterish taste, and may be usefully chewed for
#Text= tooth-ache, or to obviate paralysis of the tongue.
#Text=In Germany a variety
#Text= of this Burnet yields a blue essential oil which is used for colouring
#Text= brandy.
#Text=Again the herb is allied to the Anise (Pimpinella
#Text= Anisum).
#Text=The term Burnet was formerly applied to a brown cloth.
#Text=Smaller than this Common Burnet is the Salad Burnet, _Poterium
#Text= sanguisorba, quod sanguineos fluxus sistat_, a useful  styptic,
#Text= which is also cordial, and promotes perspiration.
#Text=It has the smell of
#Text= cucumber, and is, therefore, an ingredient of the salad bowl, or often
#Text= put into a cool tankard, whereto, says Gerard, "it gives a grace in the
#Text=taste of the plant.
#Text= good against that _malum_ of such as dwell near the German seas,
#Text= which we term the scurvie, or skirby, being used after the same
#Text= manner that watercress and scurvy-grass is used, yet is it not of so
#Text= great operation and virtue."
#Text=The leaves and stem are slightly acid
#Text= and astringent, with a somewhat bitter taste, and frequently
#Text= the former are mixed by sellers of water-cresses with their
#Text= stock-in-trade.
#Text=A full dose of the juice of fresh Brooklime is an easy purge;
#Text= and the plant has always been a popular Simple for scrofulous
#Text= affections, especially of the skin.
#Text=Chemically, this Water Pimpernel
#Text= contains some tannin, and a special bitter principle; whilst, in
#Text= common with most of the Cruciferous plants, it is endowed with a
#Text= pungent volatile oil, and some sulphur.
#Text=The bruised plant has been
#Text= applied externally for healing ulcers, burns, whitlows, and for the
#Text= mitigation of swollen piles.
#Text=The Bog Pimpernel (Anagallis tenella), is common in boggy
#Text= country, growing on watery banks, and very plentiful in the river   '   s
#Text= of Norfolk, from whence the London market is supplied.
#Text=The roots
#Text= have a warm, bitter taste, and the essential oil is highly aromatic,
#Text= this being used for preparing aromatic vinegar.
#Text=In Norfolk the
#Text= powdered dry rhizome is given for ague.
#Text=With sugar it makes an
#Text= agreeable cordial conserve.
#Text=(See _Flag (Sweet)_, _page_ 201 ).
#Text=For
#Text= preserving the aromatic qualities within the dried rhizome; or root, it
#Text= should be kept in stock unpeeled.
#Text=This contains "oleum calami," and
#Text= the bitter principle "acorin."
#Text=Some of the root may be habitually
#Text= chewed for the relief of chronic indigestion.
#Text=The odorous delights of
#Text= a pastoral time passed near these sweetly-fragrant plants have been
#Text= happily alluded to in the well-known lines of idyllic verse:--
#Text=
#Text= "Green grow the Rushes, oh!
#Text=chloride of sodium, with a little charcoal.
#Text= Garlic and Thyme, strong smelling herbs, doth beat."
#Text=Tournefort writes: "A conserve made from the flowers and leaves of
#Text= wild Thyme (Serpyllum) relieves those troubled with the falling
#Text= sickness, whilst the distilled oil promotes the monthly flow in
#Text= women."
#Text=The delicious flavour of the noted honey of Hymettus was said to be
#Text= derived from the wild Thyme there visited by the bees.
#Text=Likewise the
#Text= flesh of sheep fed on pasturage where the wild Thyme grows freely
#Text= has been said to gain a delicate flavour and taste from this source:
#Text= but herein a mistake is committed, because sheep are really averse
#Text= to such pasturage, and refuse it if they can get other food.
#Text=An infusion of the leaves of Thyme, whether wild, or cultivated,
#Text= makes an excellent aromatic tea, the odour of which is sweet and
#Text= fragrant, whilst the taste of the  plant is bitter and
#Text= camphoraceous.
